newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean union leaders face arrest, worker injured.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean union leaders face arrest, worker injured.

text.p: A South Korean worker set himself on fire in protest at a new labour law after a court, brushing aside threats of all-out strikes and appeals by an international labour group, issued arrest warrants for striking leaders.

Court officials said the warrants were issued for seven militant union leaders who have warned that any attempt to seize them will trigger nationwide work stoppages, including a public sector shutdown.

It was not immediately clear whether police would attempt to storm the grounds of Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral, where the leaders of the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions sheltered in freezing conditions inside a ramshackle tent.
Shortly after the warrants were issued, a worker set fire to himself during a clash between strikers from Hyundai Group and riot police in the southeast city of Ulsan.
The worker from Hyundai Motor Co, South Korea's biggest carmaker, was in critical condition, a Hyundai union official and hospital spokesman said.
It was the first serious injury reported since strikes erupted on December 26 when the labour bill, which allows worker layoffs for the first time, was rammed through parliament.
Earlier, confederation president Kwon Young-kil and six deputies rebuffed police trying to deliver a summons for them to appear in court.
State prosecutors had asked for the arrest of the seven on charges of obstructing business by staging illegal strikes over the introduction of the new labour law.
The judge first said he wanted to question them but issued the warrants after they refused to show up.
Police investigators supported by several hundred riot police burst into confederation headquarters shortly before midnight on Thursday and carted away documents.
"If any of the seven, including myself, are arrested, we have orders to start intensive strikes immediately," Kwon told a news conference before the warrants were issued.
South Korean's largest union body, the Federation of Korean Trade Unions, has called on workers to join the biggest strike in the nation's history for two days starting next Tuesday.
At Ulsan, Hyundai Motor shut down its plants temporarily, saying production was seriously hampered by strikes.
Hyundai workers have been at the forefront of strikes that the confederation says has brought out 190,000 of its 500,000 members. The labour ministry says only 70,000 workers are out.

A Myongdong church official urged government and union leaders to compromise, saying "democracy is the result of talks and cooperation". But he said there was nothing clergy could do if police decided to violate sacred ground to arrest the seven.

Leaders of the Brussels-based International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU) were due to arrive on Saturday to try to persuade the government to scrap a law they say is a step towards greater repression.

The head of the International Labour Organisation has written to South Korean President Kim Young-sam after the ICFTU asked him to intervene to prevent Seoul from arresting the seven, an ILO spokesman said. No other details were given.
Labour Minister Jin Nyum rejected ICFTU criticisms and said no other country had been awarding annual 15 percent pay increases while still suffering from violent industrial strife.

"There is no customer in the world who wants to buy products out of plants where petrol bombs fly because of violent labour disputes," he told a news conference. "There is nothing in the new law that worsens the rights of workers."

With strikes dragging on, many South Korea shares are at 10-year lows on valuation terms. Korean stocks were the second worst performer on the International Finance Corp's emerging market index last year.

"We are getting closer to the point where all the bad news is in the market but there could still be another wave of selling -- we haven't reached the bottom yet," said Jean De Bolle, head of strategy and global emerging market fund manger at Foreign and Colonial.
